title: Auditing 2% of calls means guessing about the other 98%
excerpt: Sampling made sense when a human had to listen to every recording. It no longer does. Here is what full-coverage auditing changes for a contact centre.
body:
Most contact centres audit a small sample of calls, often a couple of percent. The reason is practical: a quality analyst can only listen to so many recordings in a day. But the sample was never the goal. The goal is to know how every customer was treated.

What a small sample hides

  • Rare but costly events. A mis-sold product, a missed disclosure or an abusive exchange may happen on one call in a few hundred. A sample can easily miss it.
  • Agent-level patterns. With only a handful of audited calls per agent each month, one good or bad call swings the score.
  • Process gaps. If a script breaks at a particular step, you see it only when enough calls reach that step.

What changes with full coverage

When every call is transcribed and scored against the same parameters, the audit stops being a lottery. Analysts spend time on the calls that need a human: the lowest scores, the compliance flags and the escalations. Coaching conversations start from evidence across dozens of calls, not from one memorable recording.

How to start without disrupting the floor

  1. Pick the five to eight parameters you already score today: greeting, probing, resolution, tone, compliance.
  2. Run the same recordings through automated scoring and compare with your analysts' scores. Expect differences and use them to tune the parameters.
  3. Move analysts from random listening to reviewing exceptions.
  4. Report coverage as a number: the share of calls audited, next to the quality score.
Takeaway: a quality score is only as trustworthy as the share of calls behind it. Report both.

title: Voice bots vs IVR: where AI voice earns its place
excerpt: IVR menus ask customers to adapt to the system. Voice bots adapt to the customer. A practical look at where each one fits.
body:
Press 1 for billing, press 2 for support, press 3 to hear the options again. Anyone who has called a large company knows the pattern. A menu-based IVR works when choices are few and fixed. It struggles when customers describe a problem in their own words, in their own language.

Where voice bots fit best

  • Outbound reminders and confirmations such as payment due dates, appointment confirmations and delivery updates.
  • Lead qualification with a few simple questions before a salesperson calls back.
  • First-level inbound queries like order status or branch timings, where the answer already exists in a system.
  • Surveys after a service interaction, where a short spoken answer beats an ignored link.

Where people should stay in the loop

Complaints from upset customers, negotiations, and anything with legal or financial consequences deserve a human. A good bot recognises the limit and hands over with the context it has gathered, so the customer does not repeat themselves.

Questions to ask before you pilot

  1. Which languages and mixed-language speech (such as Hinglish) do your customers actually use?
  2. What happens when the bot is unsure? Is there a clean transfer to an agent?
  3. How will you measure success: completion rate, transfer rate, customer rating, cost per resolved call?
  4. Are calls disclosed as automated, and recorded in line with your consent policy?
Takeaway: start with one high-volume, low-emotion call type, measure it for a month, then expand.

title: Seven questions to ask before you switch cloud telephony providers
excerpt: Per-seat price is only one line of the bill. Use this checklist to compare providers on what actually affects your operation.
body:
Comparing cloud telephony quotes by the per-user price alone is the quickest way to be surprised later. Use these seven questions to compare like with like.

The checklist

  1. What exactly is included in the licence? Recording, reports, CRM integration and support hours are sometimes separate line items.
  2. How are channels and numbers priced as you grow? Ask for the rate to add ten more of each.
  3. Can you keep your existing numbers? Ask about porting steps and timelines.
  4. What number do customers see? A number that looks like a mobile number often gets answered more readily than an unfamiliar landline-style one.
  5. What is the uptime commitment, and what happens when it is missed? Ask to see it in writing.
  6. Where is call data stored and for how long? This matters for your own compliance obligations.
  7. How easy is it to leave? Notice periods, data export and minimum terms all count.

Run a pilot, not just a demo

Put a small team on the new system for two weeks, on real calls. Track connect rate, call quality complaints and the time agents spend on set-up tasks.

Takeaway: if a provider will not put the total monthly cost for your expected seats, channels and numbers in one quote, keep looking.

title: Five signals in your sales calls that predict revenue
excerpt: Your recordings already contain what customers want, what stops them and what competitors they mention. Here is what to listen for.
body:
Every sales call is a small research interview that most companies never read. When calls are transcribed and searchable, patterns appear that no dashboard of call counts can show.

Five signals worth tracking

  1. Objections by frequency. If price comes up on most lost calls, that is a positioning problem more than a negotiation problem.
  2. Competitor mentions. Which names come up, and in what context?
  3. Questions the agent could not answer. Each one is a training or content gap.
  4. Talk-to-listen balance. Calls where the customer does most of the talking at the discovery stage tend to progress better. Test this on your own data before you rely on it.
  5. Commitments made. Callbacks promised and not logged are lost revenue.

Turning signals into action

Review the top three objections monthly with sales and marketing together. Update the script, the website and the follow-up message in the same week, so the fix reaches customers quickly.

Takeaway: choose one signal, review it every month and change one thing as a result. Insight without a change is just reporting.

title: Outbound calling and SMS in India: a compliance primer
excerpt: Registration, templates, consent and number series: the practical basics every business should have in order before it dials or texts at scale.
body:
Businesses that call or message customers in India work within rules set by the telecom regulator, TRAI, and enforced through telecom operators. This primer summarises the basics in plain language. It is general information, not legal advice, and the rules are updated from time to time, so confirm current requirements with your telecom provider or adviser.

1. Register before you send

Commercial SMS is sent through a registered entity on the operators' DLT platform, with approved sender headers and pre-approved message templates. A message that does not match an approved template can be blocked.

2. Match the message type to the purpose

Operators distinguish between transactional, service and promotional messages and calls. A one-time password or payment alert is treated differently from an offer. Keep the purposes separate, and do not slip promotional content into a transactional template.

3. Respect consent and preferences

  • Record when and how each customer gave consent.
  • Check customer preference registers before promotional outreach.
  • Make opting out easy, and honour it promptly.

4. Use the right number series

Regulators have directed that certain kinds of calls use dedicated number series, and that promotional calling should not come from ordinary ten-digit mobile numbers. Ask your provider which series applies to your use case.

5. Keep records

Keep call logs, consent records and template approvals. If a customer complains, you will want to answer with evidence.

Takeaway: treat compliance as part of the set-up, not a clean-up. It is cheaper to get headers, templates and consent right on day one.

title: What does it really cost to audit one call?
excerpt: A simple way to compare manual quality checks with AI scoring, per call and per percentage of calls covered.
body:
Most contact centres know what they pay their quality team. Few know what each audited call costs, or how much of the operation that spend actually covers. Working that out takes ten minutes and usually changes the conversation.

Start with the manual maths

Take the monthly cost of your quality analysts, including salary, tools and the supervisor time spent on calibration. Divide it by the number of calls they audit in a month. That is your cost per audited call.

Then divide the audited calls by total calls handled. That is your coverage. A team that audits 4 calls per agent per month on a floor of 100 agents handling a few thousand calls each is looking at coverage in the low single digits.

Why cost per call is the wrong place to stop

Cost per audited call tells you how efficient the team is. It does not tell you how much you know. Two numbers matter together:

  • Cost per audited call, which tells you whether the method is affordable.
  • Coverage, which tells you how much of the operation you can actually see.

A method that is cheap per call but covers 2% of calls still leaves 98% unexamined. That is where compliance slips, rude behaviour and missed upsell moments hide.

What changes with AI scoring

AI scoring changes the shape of the cost. Manual auditing is mostly a fixed team cost that scales with headcount. AI scoring is mostly usage-based and scales with call minutes. That means coverage can move from a small sample to every call without hiring a proportionate number of analysts.

Human reviewers do not disappear. They move to the work a model cannot do alone: calibrating the scorecard, reviewing the calls flagged as risky, and coaching agents using what the scores show.

A fair way to compare

  • Write down your current cost per audited call and coverage.
  • Pick one team and run both methods on the same week of calls.
  • Compare where the two methods disagree. Those calls are the most useful ones for tuning the scorecard.
  • Decide what coverage you want, then price it.

What to ask a vendor

Ask how scoring is priced (per minute, per call or per seat), whether you can use your own scorecard, and how flagged calls reach a human. A good answer is specific about all three.

title: Hindi and Hinglish voice bots: what changes when the bot talks like your customers
excerpt: English-only bots lose a large share of Indian callers. Here is what to get right when a voice bot speaks Hindi, Hinglish or a regional language.
body:
A voice bot that only speaks formal English meets customers on its terms, not theirs. In India most callers mix languages inside a single sentence, and a bot that cannot follow them feels like a wall.

Hinglish is the default, not the exception

Many callers start a sentence in Hindi and finish it with English words for products, amounts and dates. A bot trained only on formal Hindi or only on English stumbles on exactly the words that matter: the policy name, the EMI date, the order number.

What a good Indian-language bot needs

  • Mixed-language understanding. It should handle Hindi and English words in the same utterance without asking the caller to pick one.
  • Numbers and dates in the caller's style. People say amounts and dates in many ways. The bot should accept the way people actually speak.
  • Accent range. Indian English alone covers a wide spread of accents. Test with voices from the regions you serve.
  • A natural voice. Pace, pauses and tone decide whether a caller stays on the line or hangs up in the first few seconds.
  • Regional languages where volume justifies it. Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia and Assamese each need their own testing, not a translation of the Hindi script.

Write the script for the ear

A script that reads well on a page often sounds stiff when spoken. Short sentences work better. Ask one thing at a time. Confirm what you heard before acting on it, especially numbers.

Plan the hand-off

No bot handles everything. Decide in advance which situations go to a person: anger, a complaint, a high-value customer, or two failed attempts to understand. A smooth hand-off with the conversation so far already passed on is one of the biggest drivers of caller satisfaction.

How to test before you commit

  • Call the bot yourself in the language mix your customers use.
  • Have colleagues from different regions do the same.
  • Listen for where it asks callers to repeat, and fix those points first.
  • Check the recordings for calls that ended early.

title: Voice bots for lead qualification: a playbook for auto and EV dealers
excerpt: Showroom enquiries go cold fast. A short, well-designed bot call can qualify leads, book test drives and collect feedback afterwards.
body:
A car or two-wheeler enquiry is valuable for a short time. The buyer filled in a form, asked a question on WhatsApp, or called a showroom, and then waited. Every hour of silence after that makes the sale less likely.

What a qualification call should find out

Keep the call short. Four or five questions are enough:

  • Which model or variant interests the buyer.
  • When they plan to buy: this month, this quarter, later.
  • Whether they have a car to exchange.
  • How they plan to pay: cash, loan or lease.
  • Whether they would like a test drive, and when.

A buyer who answers these goes to a salesperson with a summary. A buyer who is only browsing receives information and is called again later. The sales team spends its time on the first group.

Test drives are the point

For both petrol and electric vehicles, the test drive is the moment a buyer moves from interested to committed. The bot can offer slots, confirm one, and send a reminder the day before. A missed test drive can be rebooked with one more call.

EV buyers need a different conversation

First-time EV buyers ask about range, charging at home, charging on the road, battery warranty and running cost. A good script answers the common questions and passes the rest to a person. It should not pretend to know what it does not.

After the drive

A call a day or two after a test drive does two jobs. It asks how the drive felt and what held the buyer back, which is useful feedback for the dealer. It also reminds the buyer that a salesperson is ready to help. The same pattern works after delivery, for satisfaction (CSAT) and recommendation (NPS) questions.

Guard rails

  • Ask for consent to be contacted and record it.
  • Call at sensible hours and respect opt-outs.
  • Always give the buyer a way to speak to a person.

Measure it

Track leads called, leads reached, leads qualified, test drives booked and test drives completed. The drop between each step shows you where to improve the script.

title: CSAT and NPS by phone: how to ask without annoying customers
excerpt: Phone surveys get a richer answer than a link in an SMS, but only if the call is short, well timed and easy to leave.
body:
Customer satisfaction (CSAT) asks how a specific interaction went. Net Promoter Score (NPS) asks how likely a customer is to recommend you. Both are easier to answer in a thirty-second phone call than in a long online form, but a badly designed call does more harm than good.

Pick the right moment

Call soon enough that the customer remembers the experience, and late enough that it has actually happened. A day or two after a delivery, a service visit or a resolved complaint works for most businesses. Avoid calling during the busiest hours.

Keep it very short

One rating question and one open question is enough:

  • "On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague?"
  • "What is the main reason for your score?"

For CSAT, ask about the interaction that just happened, not the company as a whole.

Let the customer opt out

Begin by saying who is calling and why. Say how long it will take. Make it easy to decline. A customer who can say no politely is more likely to say yes next time.

The open answer is the valuable part

The number tells you the trend. The reason tells you what to fix. Record and transcribe the open answer, then group the reasons by theme: delivery, price, staff behaviour, product quality. The top two themes usually account for most of the unhappy scores.

Close the loop

Customers who gave a low score and hear nothing back learn that the survey was a formality. Route low scores to a person the same day, and tell the customer what happened.

Voice bots make this scalable

A bot can place thousands of short survey calls, in the customer's language, at the right hour, and hand a low scorer straight to an agent. Scoring and transcription happen automatically so a manager reads themes, not recordings.

Keep the data honest

Do not call only the customers you expect to be happy. Do not coach agents to ask for high scores. Compare survey scores with the satisfaction level suggested by the call itself, which is the subject of our article on perceived CSAT.

title: Perceived CSAT: reading satisfaction from the conversation itself
excerpt: Only a small share of customers answer a survey. Scoring the call itself gives you a satisfaction signal on every conversation.
body:
Most customers never answer a satisfaction survey. The ones who do tend to be either delighted or angry, so the average can look healthier or worse than reality. The call itself holds much more information, and it exists for every conversation.

What perceived CSAT means

Perceived CSAT is an estimate of how satisfied the customer was, based on what was said and how it was said during the call. It sits alongside the survey score. It does not replace it.

What the signal is made of

  • Words. Thanks, praise, and complaints are explicit signals.
  • Resolution. Was the question answered? Did the customer have to repeat themselves or call back?
  • Tone and pace. Rising pitch, long silences and interruptions often mark frustration.
  • Outcome. Did the call end with agreement, a promise, or a threat to leave?

None of these is conclusive alone. Together they give a reasonable estimate.

Where it is most useful

  • Coverage. Surveys reach a fraction of customers. A call score reaches every call.
  • Speed. You see the signal the same day, not after a survey cycle.
  • Agent coaching. Agents see which behaviours move scores on their own calls.
  • Early warning. A run of low perceived scores on one topic points to a product or process problem.

How to use it responsibly

Treat it as an estimate. Compare it with survey scores where both exist, and tune it when they disagree. Give agents a way to question a score. Do not use a single score for disciplinary decisions.

Putting it into practice

Start with the calls you already audit. Add a perceived satisfaction score to the scorecard. Review the 20 calls with the largest gap between the perceived score and the survey score. Those calls teach you the most about what your customers value.

title: Spotting fraud signals in customer calls before they become losses
excerpt: Fraud often shows up in the conversation first. Here are the patterns worth flagging, and how to act on an alert without accusing a genuine customer.
body:
Fraud attempts reach a contact centre by phone more often than many teams expect. Social engineering, account takeover attempts and false claims all depend on persuading a person. That means the conversation holds clues, if someone is listening.

Signals worth flagging

These patterns do not prove fraud. They deserve a second look:

  • A caller who cannot answer basic verification questions but pushes for a change of address, number or bank detail.
  • Urgency and pressure: "do it now", threats to escalate, claims of an emergency.
  • A call that tries one agent after another, or different identities from the same number.
  • Requests to move money, reset credentials or bypass a normal step.
  • An agent who skips verification, or shares more than the process allows.

Insider risk matters too. Calls where verification is skipped repeatedly for the same agent are worth a quiet review.

Why sampling misses it

If you audit 2% of calls, a fraudster has a 98% chance of going unseen on any single attempt. Fraud is a numbers game for the attacker. Coverage changes the odds.

How an alert should work

  • Score every call for fraud indicators, not only the ones that reached a supervisor.
  • Alert fast. A flag that arrives next week is a report. One that arrives within the hour is a defence.
  • Show the evidence. The alert should link to the exact moment in the call, with the transcript, so a reviewer can decide quickly.
  • Route it to the right team: fraud, risk or the account's manager.

Avoid harm to genuine customers

Most flagged calls are genuine. Train reviewers to verify through a trusted channel, not to accuse. Track false alarms and tune the rules so reviewers keep trusting the alerts.

Keep records

Store the flagged call, the decision and the reason. Records support investigations, regulators and agent coaching. Follow your retention policy for how long to keep them.

Where to start

Choose three patterns that matter most for your business, write them down in plain language, and run them across a month of recordings. Look at what comes back before you tune anything.

title: Catching a social media escalation before it spreads
excerpt: A complaint posted publicly can reach thousands of people within a day. A simple alert system lets your team respond while it is still one post.
body:
A customer who is ignored on the phone often says so in public. A single post, tagged with your brand, can travel a long way if it is picked up by others. The teams that handle this well are not faster at writing replies. They are faster at noticing.

Why the call centre and social media are connected

A frustrated caller who feels unheard may post that evening. A public post often starts with the words "I called three times". The call history is the context your social team needs, and the social post is the signal your call centre needs.

What an escalation alert should watch for

  • Volume. A sudden rise in mentions of your brand or a product.
  • Reach. Posts from accounts with large followings.
  • Sentiment. A run of negative posts on the same topic.
  • Keywords. Words like refund, cheated, fraud, legal, or a regulator's name.
  • Links to calls. A customer who says they called, with a number or a date you can look up.

A response plan that works

  • Decide who owns the alert, with a named person and a backup.
  • Set a target to acknowledge publicly within a few hours.
  • Move the conversation to a private channel quickly, with a single point of contact.
  • Fix the problem, then tell the customer. Close the post thread with the outcome.
  • Record the cause, and tell the team that owns it.

What not to do

  • Do not delete negative posts or argue in public.
  • Do not use the same reply for every case.
  • Do not wait for a weekly report.

Learning from the pattern

After a month, group escalations by cause: delivery, billing, product quality, agent behaviour. The top cause is usually a process problem that was visible in call recordings long before it reached social media.

Connect the two views

The best signal comes from combining them. A rise in calls about one topic, plus a rise in posts on the same topic, tells you to act today.

title: How many SIP channels do you need? A practical way to size capacity
excerpt: Too few channels and callers hear a busy tone. Too many and you pay for capacity you never use. Here is a sound way to estimate.
body:
A SIP channel is one concurrent call. If you have 30 channels, 30 calls can be in progress at the same moment, inbound or outbound. The 31st gets a busy signal or waits. Sizing channels is therefore about your busiest moment, not your average.

Start with three numbers

  • Calls per hour in your busiest hour.
  • Average call duration, including talk time and, for agents, wrap-up.
  • Your service target: how many callers may be blocked or kept waiting.

A rough starting point

Multiply calls in the busiest hour by the average duration in minutes, then divide by 60. The result is the average number of calls in progress during that hour. For example, 600 calls in an hour at an average of 5 minutes each gives 50 concurrent calls on average.

Add a safety margin for peaks within the hour and for your service target. Operations with strict targets, such as inbound support, need a larger margin than outbound campaigns where a short queue is acceptable. Telephony specialists use queueing models such as Erlang for this, and your provider can run one for you.

Inbound and outbound behave differently

Inbound demand is set by customers, and spikes follow events such as a billing cycle or an outage. Outbound demand is set by you. A dialler can place more calls than agents can handle, so outbound channels depend on your dialling ratio and answer rate, not only on agent count.

Plan for growth and seasons

  • Look at the busiest day of the last year, not an average week.
  • Add capacity ahead of known peaks: festivals, results days, renewal months.
  • Ask how quickly your provider can add channels, and whether you can scale down.

Quality matters as much as quantity

Channel count is only part of the picture. Ask about uptime commitments, how calls are routed if a route fails, and whether you can use more than one carrier path for 24/7 operations.

Questions to ask a provider

  • Is pricing per channel, per minute or both?
  • How fast can you add capacity?
  • What uptime do you commit to?
  • Can you give a quote for my volume?

title: The DPDP Act and call recordings: what contact centres should check now
excerpt: Call recordings contain personal data. A short checklist for notice, consent, retention and erasure under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
body:
Every recorded call holds a voice, often a name, a phone number and sometimes account details. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats these as personal data. The DPDP Rules were notified on 13 November 2025, and most obligations take effect on 13 May 2027. That gives contact centres a window to get ready. This article is general information, not legal advice.

Who is responsible

The business that decides why and how personal data is processed is the data fiduciary. A contact centre working for a client often acts as a data processor, following the client's instructions. Contracts should say who does what.

Notice and consent

  • Tell callers at the start of the call that it is recorded, and why.
  • Where consent is the basis for processing, it must be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, with a clear way to withdraw it.
  • Keep a record of the notice given and the consent obtained.

Collect only what you need

Do not record or transcribe more than the purpose requires. Pause recording when a caller reads out card numbers or other highly sensitive details, where your process allows.

Retention and erasure

Section 8(7) requires erasure when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served, unless another law requires the data to be kept. Set a retention period for each type of recording and transcript. Write it down. Delete on schedule, and make sure your service providers delete too. Our own windows are on the Data Retention Policy page.

Security

The Act requires reasonable security safeguards. In practice that means access controls, encryption, audit logs of who listened to which recording, and a plan for breaches. Breaches must be reported to the Data Protection Board and to affected people.

Rights of callers

People can ask what data you hold, ask for corrections, ask for erasure and complain. Decide who receives these requests and how fast you will answer.

AI and transcription

If you use AI to score or transcribe calls, the same principles apply to the transcripts and scores. Be clear in your notice that calls may be analysed with automated tools.

A practical first month

  • List every place recordings are stored.
  • Write a retention schedule.
  • Update the call-opening script.
  • Review contracts with clients and vendors.
  • Name a person responsible for requests.

title: Why OTP and promotional SMS get blocked in India, and how to fix it
excerpt: DLT registration, templates and sender headers decide whether a message arrives. A checklist for the most common causes of silent failure.
body:
You press send, the gateway says accepted, and the customer never receives the message. In India this is rarely a mystery. Telecom rules require that business messages follow a strict registration process, and anything that does not match is dropped, often without an error you can see.

The three things that must match

Under TRAI's commercial communication rules, a business sending SMS registers on the DLT (Distributed Ledger Technology) platform of each operator. Three items must line up:

  • Entity. Your registered business, with a principal entity ID.
  • Sender header. The short name the message shows as its sender. It must be registered and linked to your entity.
  • Template. The approved wording, with a content ID. The message text must match the template, with only the variable parts changed.

The most common reasons for failure

  • Wording differs slightly. An extra space, a different punctuation mark or a changed word can make the message fail template matching. Copy the approved text exactly.
  • Wrong content ID. The ID sent with the message does not belong to that template.
  • Header not mapped. The sender header is registered but not linked to the template.
  • Wrong category. A promotional message sent as a transactional or service message. Operators check this closely.
  • Variable too long or wrong type. Templates limit what may go in a variable.
  • Credentials or IP restrictions. Some gateways accept calls only from approved server addresses.
  • Number on a preference list. Promotional messages to numbers registered for preference blocking are dropped unless consent is on record.

How to debug

  • Send a test to your own number and note the time.
  • Ask your gateway for the delivery report for that message, with the operator's status code.
  • Compare the text you sent with the approved template, character by character.
  • Confirm the content ID and sender header in the DLT portal.
  • Check whether the gateway restricts by server IP.

OTP messages need extra care

An OTP has a short life, so a delayed message is as bad as a missing one. Use a transactional route, keep the text short, and never send OTPs by email or to a different number than the one being verified.

Keep records

Store the consent you hold for promotional messages, the template IDs in use and the delivery reports. They protect you if an operator or a customer asks.

If your website sends OTPs through a gateway, make sure the wording in the site matches the approved template exactly. A single changed character is enough to stop delivery.

title: Cloud telephony or an on-premise PBX? A cost and risk comparison
excerpt: Moving calling to the cloud changes where cost sits, how fast you can scale and what can go wrong. Here is a balanced comparison.
body:
Many contact centres still run an on-premise PBX, a box of hardware in a server room. Cloud telephony delivers the same job as a service. Neither is always better. The right choice depends on your size, your growth and your tolerance for risk.

Where the cost sits

  • On-premise: a large upfront purchase, then maintenance, upgrades, power, cooling, space and an engineer who knows the system. Costs are mostly fixed.
  • Cloud: a recurring fee, usually per user and per channel, with usage charges on top. Costs scale with the size of the operation.

Over three to five years, compare the total cost, not the price on the first invoice. Include the people who run the system and the cost of replacing it.

Speed and flexibility

A cloud system can add a seat or a channel in a day. Opening a new office or letting agents work from home does not need a new box. On-premise systems can be tuned deeply, but each change tends to take longer.

Reliability

On-premise systems depend on your power, your internet link and your engineer. Cloud systems depend on your internet link and your provider's resilience. Ask any provider about uptime commitments, failover routes and how outages are communicated. Have a plan for the case where your link goes down.

Features and integrations

Cloud providers update features continuously, and integrations with CRMs, dialers, call recording and analytics are usually easier. On-premise systems may need custom work for each connection.

Compliance and data

Check where recordings are stored, who can access them and how long they are kept. Ask how the provider supports consent records, retention rules and security controls that your clients expect.

Numbers and caller identity

Ask what kinds of numbers you can use and how they appear to customers. The look of the number affects whether people pick up, so test it with real calls before you commit.

A short decision guide

  • Choose cloud if you expect to grow or change, work across locations, or lack in-house telephony engineers.
  • Consider on-premise or a hybrid if you have strict data location rules, stable volumes and a capable team.
  • Run a pilot with one team before moving everyone.

Questions to ask before you switch
